grammar.title: 吗 for yes/no questions
grammar.explanation: Adding 吗 (ma) to the end of any statement turns it into a yes/no question, with no change in word order. 你好吗? means "Are you well?" This is a simpler alternative to verb-不-verb questions — don't combine the two in one sentence.

grammar.title: 呢 for follow-up questions
grammar.explanation: After stating something, 你呢? asks "and you?" without repeating the whole sentence. 呢 (ne) attaches to the topic being asked about and relies on context from what was just said.

grammar.title: 真的 for "really" and "true"
grammar.pattern: 真的 + verb/adjective, or 是真的
grammar.explanation: 真的 (zhēnde) emphasizes that something is genuinely true, either as "really" before a verb (你真的想去吗?) or as "true" after 是 (这是真的). It's a common way to react to surprising news.

grammar.title: 不用 for "no need to"
grammar.explanation: 不用 (búyòng) means there's no need to do something — softer than telling someone not to with 别. 不用了，谢谢 ("No need, thanks") is a common way to politely decline an offer.

grammar.title: 不对 for "wrong/incorrect"
grammar.explanation: 不对 (búduì) is a fixed phrase meaning "wrong" or "incorrect", used as a complete predicate on its own: 这不对 ("This is wrong"). It's a quick way to correct someone or point out a mistake.

grammar.title: 干什么 as a casual "what are you doing"
grammar.explanation: 干什么 (gànshénme) is a casual way to ask what someone is doing or up to, similar to 做什么 but more conversational. It's often paired with 在 to ask about an action in progress: 你在干什么? ("What are you doing?")

grammar.title: The five relative day words
grammar.pattern: 前天 / 昨天 / 今天 / 明天 / 后天
grammar.explanation: Chinese has a tidy set of words for days relative to today: 前天 ("the day before yesterday"), 昨天 ("yesterday"), 今天 ("today"), 明天 ("tomorrow"), 后天 ("the day after tomorrow"). Like other time words, they go at the start of the sentence or right after the subject.

grammar.title: 吧 for suggestions and requests
grammar.explanation: 吧 (ba) softens a sentence into a suggestion, request, or guess. 我们去吧 sounds like "Let's go", friendlier than a plain statement. It always comes at the very end of the sentence.

grammar.title: 别 for telling someone not to
grammar.explanation: 别 (bié) means "don't" and goes right before the verb, giving a direct instruction. Adding 了 at the end, as in 别说了, softens it to "stop doing that" rather than a flat prohibition.

sentences.en: You don't need to do it.
What do you want to do?
Are you coming the day after tomorrow?
Are you home in the evening?
Do you really want to go?
